explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says he "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done." (2 Chronicles 26:4) Amaziah was the king before him, so Uzziah had a pattern to follow. Sixteen years old and already walking straight. I can't walk straight past a cooling rack.

Not quite, friend. The text says he "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done." (2 Chronicles 26:4) So Uzziah starts out on the right path. Hold onto that, because it makes the rest of this story hit harder.

Yes, baker, success is the gift. The text says, "…as long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success." (2 Chronicles 26:5) Notice the words "…as long as…" That little phrase is carrying the whole story on its back. Keep your eye on it.

Close thinking, but no. Uzziah goes out to wage war against the Philistines in this very chapter (2 Chronicles 26:6). What the text says is that "…as long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success." (2 Chronicles 26:5) Success, not a quiet vacation from the battlefield.

Nope, friend. The text never mentions a big family here. It says "…as long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success." (2 Chronicles 26:5) Success is the gift, and it comes with that "…as long as…" attached.

That's it, baker. "Then he built cities near Ashdod and among the Philistines." (2 Chronicles 26:6) First the walls come down, then his own cities go up. Walls down, cities up, and I can't even finish a single tray of cookies without a snack break.

Not this time, friend. The text says nothing about fire. It says he "…built cities near Ashdod and among the Philistines." (2 Chronicles 26:6) He tears down, and then he builds. The only thing I burn is a batch of cookies, and that's on me.
No, baker. Idols aren't in this verse at all. The text says he "…built cities near Ashdod and among the Philistines." (2 Chronicles 26:6) Cities go up here, not idols.

Good guess, but the text says otherwise. "God helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs living in Gur-baal, and against the Meunites." (2 Chronicles 26:7) So it wasn't Uzziah's strength alone. Remember that line, because it matters later.

Right, baker. The text says, "God helped him against the Philistines, against the Arabs living in Gur-baal, and against the Meunites." (2 Chronicles 26:7) Uzziah had help, and not the small kind. Remember who the helper was: God.

Yes, baker. "…his fame spread as far as the border of Egypt, for he had become exceedingly powerful." (2 Chronicles 26:8) That's a long way for news to travel without a single group chat. Even the Ammonites were bringing him tribute. Egypt is the answer, and the reason is right there in the verse: he had become exceedingly powerful.

Not quite, friend. The text says his fame spread "…as far as the border of Egypt…" (2 Chronicles 26:8) Assyria isn't named in this verse. He had become exceedingly powerful, and Egypt's border is how far his fame reached.

Good try, baker, but no. The text says his fame spread "…as far as the border of Egypt…" (2 Chronicles 26:8) Babylon isn't named in this verse at all. That's a lot of ground for one man's name to cover, and I can barely get mine across the kitchen.

That's right, baker. The devices were made "…to shoot arrows and catapult large stones from the towers and corners." (2 Chronicles 26:15) Arrows and big stones, all from up on the towers. I can barely get a cookie off the top shelf without a stool.

Close, friend. The army did get spears (2 Chronicles 26:14), but the devices on the towers shot arrows and catapulted "large stones." (2 Chronicles 26:15) Spears were handed out to the soldiers. The stones were for the machines.

No, baker. Torches aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The devices were made "…to shoot arrows and catapult large stones from the towers and corners." (2 Chronicles 26:15) Arrows and large stones, no flames needed. If I were standing near those towers, I'd keep my hat very low.

explanations.answer: Burn incense on the altar himself
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says he "…entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense." (2 Chronicles 26:16) He went in to do it himself. The next verses show why that was a big problem.

explanations.answer: Pray for the priests serving there
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says he went in "…to burn incense on the altar of incense." (2 Chronicles 26:16) Praying for the priests isn't mentioned. He was going to do the incense job himself.

explanations.answer: Bring a gift of gold for the temple
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker. No gold shows up in this verse. He "…entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense." (2 Chronicles 26:16) That was his errand.

explanations.answer: He has no right to offer incense
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. They tell him, "Uzziah, you have no right to offer incense to the LORD." (2 Chronicles 26:18) Eighty priests plus Azariah is a whole lot of people to stand against a king. I think that took real courage.

explanations.answer: He must bring a better offering
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The priests don't say anything about a better offering. They tell him, "Uzziah, you have no right to offer incense to the LORD." (2 Chronicles 26:18) The problem was who was doing the burning.

explanations.answer: He must wait until the evening
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Timing never comes up in what the priests say. They tell him, "Uzziah, you have no right to offer incense to the LORD." (2 Chronicles 26:18) The issue was who was allowed to do it.
Not quite, baker. The priests tell him the opposite: "you will not receive honor from the LORD God." (2 Chronicles 26:18) They also say he has acted unfaithfully. So no honor is coming from this.

Right, baker. The priests tell him, "…you have acted unfaithfully; you will not receive honor from the LORD God." (2 Chronicles 26:18) That's a hard thing to say to a king's face. They said it anyway.

Yes, baker. "…leprosy broke out on his forehead." (2 Chronicles 26:19) It happened while he was raging, right there before the altar of incense. This is a heavy part of the story. I think this one hurts.
Not this one, friend. The text says "…leprosy broke out on his forehead." (2 Chronicles 26:19) A boil isn't mentioned. It's a heavy moment, and it happened while he was raging.
No, baker. The text says "…leprosy broke out on his forehead." (2 Chronicles 26:19) There's no burn here, even though he was holding a censer for incense. It was leprosy, right on his forehead.

That's right, baker. "Indeed, he himself hurried to get out, because the LORD had afflicted him." (2 Chronicles 26:20) The priests rushed him, and he was hurrying too. A king who was raging in that room is now heading for the door fast.

Not quite, friend. The text says he "…hurried to get out, because the LORD had afflicted him." (2 Chronicles 26:20) He wasn't digging in his heels. He was heading for the exit right alongside the priests.
No, baker. Begging isn't in the text. It says he "…hurried to get out, because the LORD had afflicted him." (2 Chronicles 26:20) He was moving fast, right along with the priests.

Yes, baker. "…King Uzziah was a leper until the day of his death." (2 Chronicles 26:21) It's a sober line. The text says he lived in isolation and was cut off from the house of the LORD. I think it's a hard line to read.
Not this time, friend. The text says "…King Uzziah was a leper until the day of his death." (2 Chronicles 26:21) It didn't go away. It's a heavy ending to his story.

Yes, baker. His "…son Jotham had charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land." (2 Chronicles 26:21) The kingdom still needed someone running it while Uzziah lived apart. Jotham stepped up.

Close, friend, since Azariah is a big name in this story. But the text says it was Uzziah's "son Jotham" who "…had charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land." (2 Chronicles 26:21) Azariah was the chief priest who went in after Uzziah along with eighty priests. (2 Chronicles 26:17, 20)

Not quite, baker. Hananiah, one of the royal officers, was named earlier in connection with the army records (2 Chronicles 26:11). The one who "…had charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land." was Uzziah's son Jotham. (2 Chronicles 26:21)

explanations.answer: In a burial field of the kings
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. He was "…buried near them in a field of burial that belonged to the kings, for the people said, “He was a leper.”…" (2 Chronicles 26:23) So he was laid near the kings, but in a field. That's how his story closes.

explanations.answer: In the courts of the temple
explanations.explanation: No, friend. The text says he was "…cut off from the house of the LORD…" (2 Chronicles 26:21), and he was buried "…in a field of burial that belonged to the kings…" (2 Chronicles 26:23) The temple courts aren't mentioned. The kings' field is where he was laid.
Not quite, baker. Lachish isn't mentioned in this passage. He was buried "…near them in a field of burial that belonged to the kings…" (2 Chronicles 26:23) The kings' own field is the answer.
